prosecution_strengths: New Jersey's per se BAC standard of 0.08 allows conviction without proving actual impairment if chemical test results are properly obtained.
There is no jury trial right for DWI in NJ — cases are tried in municipal court before a judge, typically resulting in faster convictions.
defense_opportunities: Challenge the legality of the traffic stop — without reasonable articulable suspicion, all evidence from the stop may be suppressed.
Challenge the 20-minute observation period before breath testing — any deviation can render results inadmissible.
Challenge field sobriety test administration under standardized NHTSA protocols.
common_defenses: Improper stop — the officer lacked reasonable articulable suspicion to initiate the traffic stop.
Faulty Alcotest — the breath testing device was not properly calibrated, maintained, or operated.
Observation period violation — the mandatory 20-minute observation period before breath testing was not properly conducted.
Rising BAC defense — defendant's blood alcohol was below 0.08 at the time of actual operation.
Medical condition — GERD, diabetes, or other medical conditions produced false high BAC readings.

prosecution_strengths: New Jersey has no statute of limitations on prior DWI offenses for enhancement purposes — convictions from any time prior count.
Step-down provisions only allow leniency if 10+ years pass between convictions, making most repeat cases ineligible for relief.
IDRC (Intoxicated Driver Resource Center) attendance is mandatory and adds significant burden beyond direct penalties.
defense_opportunities: Challenge whether 10 years have passed since the prior conviction to invoke step-down provisions.
Challenge the chemical test results following the same Chun protocol attacks available for first offense.
Argue for inpatient or outpatient treatment in lieu of certain jail components.
common_defenses: Laurick challenge — prior DWI conviction was obtained without counsel and cannot be used for enhancement.
Step-down eligibility — more than 10 years have passed since the prior conviction, allowing first-offense treatment.
Improper stop or observation period violation.

prosecution_strengths: License revocation of 8 years and ignition interlock requirement create severe long-term consequences.
Third offense is still a traffic violation in NJ (not a criminal offense), but the jail sentence is mandatory and cannot be suspended.
Prior DWI convictions from any state with equivalent statutes count for enhancement purposes.
defense_opportunities: Challenge prior convictions through Laurick — uncounseled priors cannot enhance the current offense.
Challenge the equivalency of out-of-state DWI priors used for enhancement.
Argue for the maximum 90 days of inpatient treatment in lieu of jail time.
Challenge the chemical test results and the legality of the stop under the same standards as first offense.
common_defenses: Laurick challenge — prior conviction was uncounseled and invalid for enhancement purposes.
Out-of-state prior not equivalent — the prior conviction does not meet New Jersey's statutory equivalency standard.
Faulty Alcotest under Chun protocol.
Illegal stop — no reasonable articulable suspicion to initiate the traffic stop.

prosecution_strengths: Positive toxicology for any prohibited substance combined with observed impairment supports conviction.
Even legally prescribed medications can form the basis of a DWI-drugs charge if they impair driving ability.
defense_opportunities: Challenge the DRE officer's qualifications and protocol compliance under the 12-step DRE evaluation standard.
Argue that drug metabolites in the system do not prove active impairment at the time of driving.
Challenge the connection between observed driving and the alleged drug impairment.
Highlight the lack of a per se threshold, making the case dependent on subjective officer observations.
common_defenses: No active impairment — drug metabolites were present but not causing impairment at the time of driving.
Legitimate prescription — medication was taken as prescribed without warning of impairment.
Faulty DRE evaluation — protocol was not properly followed or officer lacked certification.
Alternative explanation — observed symptoms were caused by fatigue, illness, or medical condition.

prosecution_strengths: No Early Release Act (NERA) requires 85% of the sentence to be served for vehicular homicide convictions.
Reckless driving causing death satisfies the elements — proof of recklessness is the key contested issue.
Toxicology evidence linking impairment to the accident creates powerful circumstantial proof.
defense_opportunities: Challenge whether the defendant's conduct rose to the level of recklessness rather than mere negligence.
Retain accident reconstruction experts to demonstrate alternative causes of the collision.
Challenge the toxicology evidence and its connection to actual impairment at the time of the accident.
Negotiate for downgraded charges (assault by auto) where causation evidence is weak.
common_defenses: Independent intervening cause — the death resulted from factors unrelated to the defendant's driving.
Not reckless — defendant's conduct was negligent but did not rise to criminal recklessness.
Lack of impairment — toxicology does not establish impairment at the time of the collision.
Victim contributory factors — victim's own actions were the proximate cause of death.

prosecution_strengths: Combining DWI evidence with injury evidence creates a strong narrative of consequence.
Medical evidence of victim injuries provides objective proof of harm.
Civil liability and victim restitution add pressure for plea negotiations.
defense_opportunities: Challenge causation — argue the injury would have occurred regardless of impairment.
Challenge the underlying DWI evidence using Chun protocol attacks.
Retain accident reconstruction experts to dispute the prosecution's theory.
Argue for downgrade to standard DWI plus civil liability where evidence of injury causation is weak.
common_defenses: No causation — the injury was not caused by the defendant's impairment.
Faulty DWI evidence — challenge breath test results under Chun protocol.
Independent cause — the injury resulted from victim's own conduct or third-party action.
Improper stop — the underlying traffic stop was unconstitutional.

prosecution_strengths: Officer testimony, dashcam footage, and witness statements typically establish the driving pattern.
Reckless driving is a traffic offense without jury trial, decided by municipal court judges.
Often charged alongside other offenses to increase plea leverage.
defense_opportunities: Challenge whether the conduct was 'willful or wanton' versus merely negligent or careless.
Present evidence of road conditions, weather, or emergency that explains the driving.
Challenge the officer's ability to accurately observe and characterize the driving pattern.
common_defenses: Not willful or wanton — conduct was at most negligent, not the gross deviation required for reckless driving.
Emergency circumstances — defendant was responding to a medical or safety emergency.
Inaccurate observation — officer could not reliably observe the driving from their vantage point.
Downgrade to careless — the conduct supports careless driving at most, not reckless.

prosecution_strengths: DMV records definitively establish suspension status and presumed notice.
Suspended driving following DWI carries enhanced mandatory penalties including jail time.
Repeat offenders face mandatory minimum jail under fourth-degree charges.
defense_opportunities: Challenge whether the defendant received actual notice of the suspension.
Challenge the underlying suspension if it was administratively defective.
Argue good faith belief that the suspension had been lifted.
Challenge the identification of the defendant as the driver.
common_defenses: Lack of notice — defendant never received notification of the suspension.
Administrative error — DMV records were incorrect.
Good faith belief — defendant reasonably believed the license was reinstated.
Necessity — drove in response to an urgent emergency.

prosecution_strengths: Following CREAMMA, possession over legal limits or by minors remains criminal.
Possession in a motor vehicle outside of original packaging may still draw charges in certain contexts.
defense_opportunities: Challenge whether the amount was within legalized possession limits under CREAMMA.
Challenge the search that produced the marijuana — odor of marijuana alone is no longer probable cause for vehicle searches in NJ.
Challenge the chain of custody for the alleged residue testing.
Argue the marijuana belonged to another person in shared space.
common_defenses: Within legal limits — possession was within the amounts permitted by CREAMMA for personal use.
Illegal search — marijuana odor alone does not justify a vehicle search post-CREAMMA.
Lack of possession — the marijuana belonged to someone else in the shared space.
Inaccurate weight — the substance was weighed improperly.

prosecution_strengths: Constructive possession doctrine permits conviction when drugs are in shared spaces with knowledge and ability to control.
Mandatory drug testing and forfeiture provisions add pressure beyond direct sentence.
PTI (Pretrial Intervention) eligibility provides leverage but requires admission of conduct.
defense_opportunities: Challenge the legality of the search through suppression motions.
Challenge constructive possession in shared spaces.
Pursue Pretrial Intervention (PTI) under R. 3:28 for first-time offenders.
common_defenses: Illegal search and seizure — no probable cause or warrant exception.
Lack of knowledge — defendant was unaware of the substance's presence.
Constructive possession failure — drugs were in shared space and cannot be attributed to defendant.
Substance identity — the material is not a controlled substance or testing was flawed.

prosecution_strengths: Quantity thresholds create per se intent presumptions — possession of certain weights establishes intent without other evidence.
Brimage Guidelines structure plea offers based on weight, drug type, and prior record.
defense_opportunities: Challenge the 'intent' element by arguing the quantity was consistent with personal use.
Challenge the school zone measurements and the validity of the drug-free zone designation.
Challenge the search that produced the evidence.
common_defenses: Personal use — quantity and circumstances were consistent with personal consumption.
Illegal search — evidence obtained through unconstitutional search.
No distribution evidence — absence of scales, baggies, or large cash undermines intent inference.
School zone challenge — the location was not actually within the prohibited zone.

prosecution_strengths: Wiretap evidence, controlled buys, and cooperator testimony build comprehensive cases against network leaders.
Brimage Guidelines mandate harsh plea offers in trafficking cases.
defense_opportunities: Challenge the 'leader' designation — argue the defendant was a participant, not an organizer.
Challenge cooperator credibility and motive to fabricate.
Pursue Drug Court if otherwise eligible despite the trafficking charge.
common_defenses: Not a leader — defendant was a participant, not an organizer of the alleged network.
Entrapment — government agents induced the defendant's participation.
Illegal wiretap — electronic surveillance was not properly authorized.
Unreliable cooperator — testifying witnesses are fabricating to secure their own pleas.

prosecution_strengths: Drug residue on paraphernalia provides direct evidence of use.
Often added to drug possession charges to increase total exposure.
Broad statutory definition covers a wide range of items.
defense_opportunities: Argue the item has lawful purposes (tobacco, kitchen scales, plastic bags).
Challenge the 'intent to use' element.
Challenge the legality of the search.
Argue the paraphernalia belonged to another person.
common_defenses: Lawful purpose — item is commonly used for legal purposes.
No intent — no evidence of intent to use with controlled substances.
Illegal search — paraphernalia discovered through unconstitutional search.
Lack of possession — item belonged to someone else.

prosecution_strengths: Life without parole available for aggravated cases.
Forensic evidence (DNA, ballistics, digital forensics) provides powerful physical proof in modern investigations.
Premeditation evidence is often documented through electronic communications.
defense_opportunities: Challenge purpose or knowledge — argue reckless conduct supporting reduction to manslaughter.
Challenge forensic evidence through independent expert analysis.
Challenge eyewitness identifications.
common_defenses: Passion/provocation manslaughter — killing was in response to adequate provocation.
Misidentification — defendant was not the perpetrator.
Diminished capacity — mental health condition prevented the formation of purpose or knowledge.
Defense of others — defendant acted to protect another person.

prosecution_strengths: Felony murder requires no proof of intent to kill, only participation in the predicate felony.
Mandatory 30-year minimum before parole eligibility.
Co-defendant testimony often establishes participation in the underlying felony.
defense_opportunities: Challenge participation in the underlying felony.
Argue the death was not within the foreseeable consequences of the felony.
Argue the defendant withdrew from the felony before the death occurred.
common_defenses: Affirmative defense — defendant did not commit the homicidal act, was not armed, did not solicit it, and had no reason to believe others were armed.
Withdrawal — defendant withdrew from the underlying felony before the death.
Not a participant — defendant was not involved in the underlying felony.
Death not in furtherance — the death was not connected to the felonious conduct.

prosecution_strengths: First-degree crime with NERA 85% requirement.
Lower mens rea than murder makes it easier to prove than purposeful killing.
Often charged as a lesser included offense to murder, providing jury compromise option.
defense_opportunities: Challenge the 'extreme indifference' element to reduce to standard reckless manslaughter.
Present evidence of passion/provocation reducing culpability.
Challenge causation through forensic experts.
Argue self-defense or imperfect self-defense.
common_defenses: Self-defense — used force to protect against imminent threat.
Passion/provocation — adequate provocation reduced culpability.
Not extreme indifference — conduct was reckless but did not show extreme disregard for life.
Accident — death was unintended.

prosecution_strengths: BAC of 0.08+ creates a presumption of recklessness under the statute.
Reckless driving without alcohol can still support the charge with sufficient evidence.
Toxicology and accident reconstruction provide objective evidence.
defense_opportunities: Challenge recklessness — argue the conduct was negligent at most.
Challenge causation through accident reconstruction.
Challenge toxicology and the chain from drinking to driving to crash.
Argue intervening cause.
common_defenses: Not reckless — conduct was negligent, not the gross deviation required for criminal liability.
Intervening cause — a separate event caused the death.
Victim negligence — victim's own conduct was the proximate cause.
No causal connection to impairment — the accident would have occurred regardless of BAC.

prosecution_strengths: Disorderly persons offense (max 6 months), but elevation possible based on context.
Victim testimony alone can support conviction.
Photographs of injuries are compelling evidence.
defense_opportunities: Challenge victim credibility and motive to fabricate.
Argue accidental contact or mutual combat.
common_defenses: Self-defense — used force in response to imminent threat.
Mutual combat — both parties willingly engaged in physical altercation.
Accidental contact — touching was unintentional.
False accusation — alleged victim fabricated the incident.

prosecution_strengths: Grading from second degree (5-10 years) to fourth degree depending on circumstances.
Second-degree aggravated assault carries NERA 85% requirement.
Medical records of victim injuries provide objective proof.
defense_opportunities: Challenge whether injuries meet 'serious bodily injury' definition (substantial risk of death, protracted impairment).
Challenge identification and witness credibility.
Argue for downgrade to simple assault if aggravating elements are weak.
common_defenses: Self-defense — defended against imminent serious bodily harm.
Defense of others — protected a third party.
Misidentification — defendant was not the assailant.
Mutual combat — both parties were willing participants.
Injuries not serious — failed to meet statutory threshold.

prosecution_strengths: The deadly weapon element transforms simple assault into a felony-level offense.
Physical evidence of the weapon plus victim injuries creates strong proof.
defense_opportunities: Argue self-defense including defensive use of weapons.
Challenge whether injuries were caused by the weapon versus other means.
If a firearm, pursue Graves Act waiver where eligible.
common_defenses: Self-defense — used the weapon to protect against imminent threat.
Not a deadly weapon — object does not meet statutory definition.
Misidentification — defendant was not the assailant.
Accidental — injury was not caused by intentional use of the weapon.

prosecution_strengths: NERA 85% requirement applies to all robbery convictions.
Even minimal force (a push, grab) satisfies the element.
Surveillance footage and victim identification commonly available.
defense_opportunities: Challenge identification through eyewitness reliability arguments.
Argue the taking was theft without force, reducing to a lesser offense.
Challenge whether the force was used 'in the course of' the theft.
Argue claim of right — defendant believed the property was theirs.
common_defenses: Misidentification — defendant was not the robber.
No force used — taking was theft, not robbery.
Claim of right — defendant believed they had a right to the property.
Alibi — defendant was elsewhere at the time.

prosecution_strengths: NERA 85% requirement applies.
Display of any object reasonably believed to be a deadly weapon satisfies the element.
Forensic evidence (DNA, fingerprints, ballistics) frequently links the defendant to the weapon.
defense_opportunities: Challenge whether the object displayed was actually a weapon or reasonably perceived as one.
Challenge identification, particularly with disguises or brief encounters.
Argue duress — defendant was forced to participate by a co-defendant.
Challenge the chain of custody on weapon and forensic evidence.
common_defenses: Misidentification — defendant was not involved.
No weapon — defendant did not possess or display a weapon.
Duress — defendant was coerced to participate.
False co-defendant testimony — co-defendant is falsely implicating the defendant.

prosecution_strengths: NERA 85% requirement applies, with potential 25-year mandatory minimum for child victims.
Victim testimony about confinement is powerful evidence.
Electronic evidence (cell location, surveillance, GPS) corroborates movement and detention.
defense_opportunities: Challenge the 'unlawful removal' element — argue movement was voluntary or incidental.
Argue the victim went voluntarily.
Challenge the purpose element — argue the conduct does not match any statutory purpose.
Argue any movement was incidental to another offense.
common_defenses: Consent — alleged victim went voluntarily.
No criminal purpose — restraint did not serve any prohibited purpose.
Incidental movement — movement was incidental to another crime.
Misidentification — defendant was not involved.

prosecution_strengths: NERA 85% requirement applies.
Surveillance footage from the area is increasingly common.
Vehicle GPS systems frequently lead to rapid recovery and identification.
defense_opportunities: Challenge identification.
Argue the vehicle was unoccupied at the time of taking.
Argue duress.
Challenge whether force or threat was actually used.
common_defenses: Misidentification — defendant was not the carjacker.
Vehicle unoccupied — taking does not meet the carjacking definition.
No force — the taking did not involve violence or threat.
Duress — defendant acted under coercion.

prosecution_strengths: Unauthorized entry alone, without force, satisfies the element.
Forensic evidence at entry points links defendants to the scene.
Possession of stolen property creates strong inference of involvement.
defense_opportunities: Challenge the 'purpose to commit an offense' — argue innocent entry purpose.
Challenge identification and forensic evidence.
Argue authorized entry or reasonable belief of authorization.
Challenge whether the structure qualifies under the statute.
common_defenses: No criminal purpose — entered for innocent reasons.
Authorized entry — had permission to enter.
Misidentification — was not the person who entered.
Alibi — was elsewhere when the burglary occurred.

prosecution_strengths: NERA 85% requirement applies if injury or threat is involved.
Resident/victim testimony about the invasion is powerful evidence.
Forensic evidence inside the home directly links the defendant.
defense_opportunities: Challenge whether the structure was actually occupied at the time of entry.
Challenge identification through forensic and witness evidence.
Argue authorized entry or mistaken address.
Challenge the 'purpose to commit an offense' element.
common_defenses: Not occupied — the structure was unoccupied at the time of entry.
Authorized entry — had permission or believed they did.
Misidentification — was not the person who entered.
No criminal purpose — entered for innocent reasons.

prosecution_strengths: Grading by value: under $200 disorderly persons; $200-$500 fourth degree; $500-$75,000 third degree; $75,000+ second degree.
Surveillance, possession of stolen property, and witness testimony are common evidence.
Aggregation rules allow combining multiple thefts to reach felony thresholds.
defense_opportunities: Argue claim of right.
Challenge the valuation to reduce charge grade.
Argue mistaken taking.
Argue consent.
common_defenses: Claim of right — believed in good faith they had a right to the property.
Mistake — took the wrong item by accident.
Consent — owner permitted the taking.
Valuation dispute — actual value is below felony threshold.

prosecution_strengths: VIN tracking and modern vehicle GPS lead to rapid recovery and identification.
Forensic evidence inside the vehicle directly links defendants.
Surveillance footage from parking areas captures the taking.
defense_opportunities: Argue permission to use the vehicle.
Challenge identification.
Argue joyriding/intent to return rather than permanent deprivation.
Argue good faith purchase.
common_defenses: Permission — had owner's consent.
Joyriding — intended to return the vehicle.
Misidentification — was not the thief.
Good faith purchase — bought through what appeared legitimate.

prosecution_strengths: Loss prevention testimony combined with surveillance footage provides direct evidence.
Repeat shoplifting can be aggregated for higher offense grading.
Civil recovery provisions add financial pressure beyond criminal penalties.
defense_opportunities: Challenge the presumption — argue inadvertent concealment.
Challenge surveillance interpretation.
Argue intent to pay before reaching the register.
common_defenses: No intent to steal — planned to pay.
Inadvertent concealment — accidentally placed in bag.
Misidentification — wrong person identified.
Already paid — believed item was previously paid for.

prosecution_strengths: Aggravated arson (causing serious injury or substantial damage) is a first-degree crime.
Fire investigators can determine origin and cause with high reliability.
Insurance fraud motive evidence is powerful in arson-for-profit cases.
defense_opportunities: Challenge the fire investigation methodology.
Retain independent fire investigation experts.
Argue accidental fire causes.
Challenge the 'purpose' element.
common_defenses: Accidental fire — natural, electrical, or mechanical cause.
Misidentification — did not start the fire.
Faulty investigation — origin/cause determination is unreliable.
Lack of intent — did not knowingly start the fire.

prosecution_strengths: Felony grading at $500+ damage; over $2,000 is third degree.
Photographic evidence and repair estimates are straightforward.
Surveillance footage often captures the act.
defense_opportunities: Challenge valuation to reduce grade.
Argue accidental damage.
Challenge identification.
Argue right to alter the property.
common_defenses: Accident — damage was unintentional.
Misidentification — was not the person who caused damage.
Right to alter — had legal authority over the property.
Valuation dispute — actual cost is less than alleged.

prosecution_strengths: Mandatory arrest for primary aggressor with probable cause.
Civil restraining orders (FROs) carry collateral consequences and may proceed even if criminal charges are dropped.
Excited utterance and 911 statements admissible regardless of victim cooperation.
defense_opportunities: Challenge identification of primary aggressor.
Present evidence of self-defense.
Challenge recanted statements and witness motive.
Argue mutual combat.
common_defenses: Self-defense — defended against the alleged victim.
False allegation — fabricated for divorce/custody advantage.
Mutual combat — both parties were aggressors.
Accidental contact — injuries were not intentionally caused.

prosecution_strengths: Pattern of conduct established with as few as two acts.
Electronic evidence comprehensively documents unwanted contact.
Victim testimony about fear is sympathetic and powerful.
defense_opportunities: Challenge whether the conduct caused 'reasonable fear.'
Argue legitimate purpose for contacts.
Challenge whether conduct constitutes a 'course of conduct.'
Present evidence the alleged victim welcomed contacts.
common_defenses: Legitimate purpose — contacts were for lawful reasons.
No reasonable fear — conduct would not cause a reasonable person to fear.
Isolated incidents — not a course of conduct.
Consent — victim was a willing participant.

prosecution_strengths: FROs in NJ are permanent unless lifted by court order, creating long-term liability.
Service of the FRO creates documented notice.
Electronic evidence definitively proves contact violations.
defense_opportunities: Challenge service of the FRO.
Argue victim-initiated contact.
Challenge the scope of the order.
Argue accidental encounter in public.
common_defenses: No service — never received the FRO.
Victim-initiated contact — protected person made first contact.
Accidental encounter — public coincidence.
Outside scope — conduct not actually prohibited by the order.

prosecution_strengths: DCP&P (Division of Child Protection and Permanency) reports provide investigative documentation.
Medical evidence of non-accidental trauma is devastating.
Children's recorded forensic interviews provide detailed accounts.
defense_opportunities: Retain independent medical experts to challenge non-accidental trauma findings.
Challenge the reliability of child statements through suggestibility analysis.
Present alternative perpetrator evidence.
Argue accidental injury consistent with normal childhood activity.
common_defenses: Accidental injury — childhood activity caused injuries.
Alternative perpetrator — another caregiver caused the harm.
Medical explanation — underlying condition mimics abuse.
Unreliable child statement — coached or suggestive interviewing.

prosecution_strengths: DCP&P investigations create documented evidence.
Medical evidence of malnutrition or untreated conditions is compelling.
Teacher and neighbor testimony establishes home environment.
defense_opportunities: Argue parenting was within reasonable discretion.
Present overall caregiving evidence.
Challenge DCP&P investigation methodology.
Show remediation of any deficient conditions.
common_defenses: Adequate care — within reasonable parenting standards.
Lack of knowledge — unaware of the condition.
Remediation — promptly corrected when discovered.
Cultural difference — practices are within accepted norms.

prosecution_strengths: Public records of prior conviction make proof straightforward.
Constructive possession permits conviction for weapons in shared spaces.
defense_opportunities: Challenge whether the prior conviction qualifies as a predicate.
Challenge constructive possession in shared spaces.
Pursue Graves Act waiver where eligible.
Challenge the search.
common_defenses: No qualifying prior — prior conviction does not meet predicate requirements.
Not in possession — weapon belonged to another in shared space.
Illegal search — weapon discovered through unconstitutional search.
Annulment or expungement — prior was cleared, restoring rights.

prosecution_strengths: NJ has very strict carry permit requirements; unpermitted possession is presumptively illegal.
Possession in public space without proper documentation is straightforward to prove.
Even temporary possession can satisfy the element.
defense_opportunities: Challenge the search that produced the firearm.
Pursue Graves Act waiver where eligible.
Argue the defendant had a valid permit or exception.
common_defenses: Valid permit — defendant had a carry permit at the time.
Statutory exception — possession qualified under one of the statutory exceptions (transport, hunting, range).
Illegal search — firearm discovered through unconstitutional search.
Temporary lawful possession — defendant was transporting in compliance with law.

prosecution_strengths: Applies to a wide range of firearm-related offenses.
Mandatory parole ineligibility severely restricts plea negotiations.
Limited Graves Act waivers available only with prosecutor consent.
defense_opportunities: Pursue Graves Act waiver — must be approved by the assignment judge.
Challenge the underlying firearm possession or use evidence.
Argue the firearm is not operable or does not meet the statutory definition.
Negotiate for non-firearm charges that avoid the Graves Act trigger.
common_defenses: Not a firearm — object does not meet statutory definition or is inoperable.
Illegal search — firearm evidence should be suppressed.
Graves Act waiver — eligible for waiver based on circumstances.
No possession or use — defendant did not actually possess or use the firearm.

prosecution_strengths: Graves Act minimums apply.
Forensic evidence of firearm use (ballistics, gunshot residue) is powerful.
Multiple charges create plea leverage.
defense_opportunities: Challenge ballistics and gunshot residue evidence.
Argue self-defense.
Pursue Graves Act waiver.
Challenge the search and seizure of the firearm.
common_defenses: Self-defense — used firearm against imminent threat.
Misidentification — was not the shooter.
No firearm — challenge whether a firearm was actually used.
Illegal search — firearm evidence should be suppressed.

prosecution_strengths: Digital evidence and financial records provide comprehensive proof.
IP addresses and device identifiers link defendants to fraudulent activity.
Multiple victim cases increase exposure substantially.
defense_opportunities: Challenge the identification of the defendant as the user.
Argue authorization from the alleged victim.
Challenge forensic evidence linking defendant to transactions.
Argue defendant was a victim of identity theft as well.
common_defenses: Authorization — victim gave permission to use identity information.
Mistaken identity — someone else used defendant's devices.
No fraudulent purpose — used information for non-fraudulent reasons.
Defendant also a victim — defendant's identity was compromised by a third party.

prosecution_strengths: Transaction records precisely document each unauthorized use.
Surveillance frequently captures the user.
Multiple transactions create aggregated value supporting felony grading.
defense_opportunities: Argue authorization from the cardholder.
Challenge identification.
Challenge digital forensics linking defendant to online use.
Argue lack of fraudulent intent.
common_defenses: Authorization — cardholder permitted use.
Misidentification — someone else used the card.
Lack of intent — believed they had authorization.
Found card — discovered abandoned card without intent to defraud.

prosecution_strengths: Insurance Fraud Prosecutor's Office has dedicated resources for these cases.
Surveillance contradicting claimed injuries is devastating.
Pattern evidence across multiple claims demonstrates intent.
defense_opportunities: Argue good faith claim based on honest understanding.
Challenge surveillance interpretation.
Present independent medical evidence.
Argue agent error in documentation.
common_defenses: Good faith — genuinely believed claim was accurate.
Agent error — agent misdocumented statements.
Legitimate injury — medical condition is real.
No material misrepresentation — inaccuracies were not material.

prosecution_strengths: Forensic accounting can trace every diverted dollar.
Employment records establish position of trust.
Pattern evidence demonstrates intent over time.
defense_opportunities: Argue authorization for the transactions.
Challenge forensic accounting methodology.
Argue intent to repay (loan).
Challenge valuation.
common_defenses: Authorization — was authorized to make the transactions.
Accounting error — discrepancies result from bookkeeping errors.
Intent to repay — treated funds as a loan.
Claim of right — believed entitled to the funds.

prosecution_strengths: Megan's Law registration applies.
DNA evidence and SANE examinations provide physical proof.
Child witnesses receive special protections in court.
defense_opportunities: Challenge DNA evidence and chain of custody.
Present consent defense (where age permits).
Challenge identification through expert testimony on memory reliability.
Challenge child witness statements through suggestibility analysis.
common_defenses: Consent — sexual contact was consensual between adults.
Misidentification — defendant was not the perpetrator.
False accusation — fabricated for personal motive.
Insufficient evidence — physical evidence does not support the alleged conduct.

prosecution_strengths: Megan's Law registration applies.
Victim testimony combined with forensic evidence is powerful.
No statute of limitations for many sexual assault charges in NJ.
defense_opportunities: Challenge consent and capacity issues.
Challenge forensic evidence interpretation.
Present prior consensual relationship evidence where relevant.
Challenge identification.
common_defenses: Consent — contact was consensual.
Misidentification — was not the perpetrator.
False accusation — fabricated allegation.
No knowledge of incapacity — did not know victim was incapacitated.

prosecution_strengths: Lower burden than penetration cases — only contact element required.
Victim testimony alone can support conviction.
Pattern evidence may be admissible.
defense_opportunities: Challenge whether the contact was sexual in nature.
Argue consent.
Challenge identification.
Argue accidental contact.
common_defenses: Consent — contact was consensual.
Not sexual — contact was incidental and non-sexual.
Misidentification — was not the person involved.
Accidental — contact was unintentional.

prosecution_strengths: Lowest grade sexual contact offense, but conviction still has serious collateral consequences.
Victim testimony alone can suffice.
Often used as plea offer reduction from higher charges.
defense_opportunities: Argue consent.
Challenge whether the contact was sexual.
Challenge identification.
Pursue Pretrial Intervention if eligible.
common_defenses: Consent — contact was consensual.
Not sexual — contact was incidental.
Misidentification — wrong person identified.
Accidental contact — unintentional touching.

prosecution_strengths: Disorderly persons offense for ordinary lewdness, fourth degree if exposed to children under 13.
Witness testimony is straightforward.
Repeat offenders face Megan's Law registration.
defense_opportunities: Argue accidental exposure.
Challenge witness identification and reliability.
Argue privacy expectation in the location.
Challenge intent element.
common_defenses: Accidental — wardrobe malfunction or bathroom emergency.
Privacy — defendant had a reasonable expectation of privacy.
No sexual purpose — exposure was not for arousal.
